speech_verification.heard: In 1907, inspectors measured a bending steel cord on the Quebec bridge. Designing engineer Peter Schlapka drafted the lower cords with a defective design. Consulting engineer Theodore Cooper officially approved these flawed plans. Officials placed complete confidence in Cooper's judgment. But contemporary professional knowledge of steel columns under load was inadequate. By August 27, no action could prevent the structural collapse. — yet better judgment could have saved human lives on the site.

corroboration.heard: In 1907, inspectors measured a bending steel cord on the Quebec Bridge. Designing engineer Peter Schlapka drafted the lower cords with a defective design. Consulting engineer Theodore Cooper officially approved these flawed plans. Officials placed complete confidence in Cooper's judgment. But contemporary professional knowledge of steel columns under load was inadequate. By August 27, no action could prevent the structural collapse. yet better judgment could have saved human lives on the site.

notes.hook: The hook is too passive, stating that inspectors merely 'measured' the bend rather than emphasizing the impending danger.
notes.clarity: The narrative doesn't clearly connect why the warnings were ignored or how the design flaws led directly to the collapse.
notes.payoff: The ending feels abrupt and lacks a strong dramatic punch, mentioning saved lives without fully delivering on the tragedy's climax.
notes.visuals: Using four text-only title cards in a row is visually unengaging and lazy for a highly visual medium.
notes.loop: The transition from the final line back to the opening line is grammatically clunky and fails to create a seamless loop.

Beat 7: Many human lives would have been saved, if they hadn't ignored how...
rounds.better_than_last: This Short focuses on a compelling, slow-burn engineering disaster, though its heavy reliance on text cards makes it less visually engaging than the recent Arnhem episode.
